html:
Control primitives are organized along multiple brain gradients. The principal cortical gradient of connectivity runs from unimodal sensory-motor areas to transmodal association cortex (especially default-mode areas) 1. Unimodal regions handle immediate sensory-driven control (fast stimulus-response gating), whereas at the transmodal apex (e.g. frontopolar, DMN) lie abstract, context-rich representations. In practice, this means that simple reactive control operations predominate in peripheral cortex, whereas high-level rule integration and counterfactual reasoning occur in frontopolar/dorsomedial PFC. Gradients of neural timescale parallel this axis: primary sensory and motor areas have very short intrinsic timescales (rapid dynamics), while PFC and other association areas integrate information over seconds or longer 2. These gradations shape control: a top-down signal from frontopolar cortex can modulate a very slow-changing goal context, whereas a sensory cortex only can sustain fast-varying cues. In other words, cortex has a built-in hierarchy of time constants, so that control primitives operating at different levels naturally inherit different temporal resolutions. A 2026 preprint maps cortical intrinsic timescales (Figure) 27. The preprint examines developmental trajectories (Figure).

Within frontal cortex, multiple orthogonal gradients shape what is represented and controlled. Along the rostro-caudal axis, evidence supports a hierarchy of abstraction: caudal premotor and posterior lateral PFC carry concrete sensorimotor plans and stimulus-response mappings (e.g., effector- and spatially specific codes used to implement a learned rule), mid-dlPFC encodes conditional/task rules and context-dependent mappings (e.g., "if color then compare, if motion then ignore"), and the most anterior territories (rostrolateral/frontopolar cortex) integrate across time and tasks, representing pending subgoals, alternative strategies, and higher-order relations among rules 3, 4, 5. For example, frontopolar/RLPFC tracks the value of unchosen options and supports exploratory strategy switches-representations that sit "above" the immediate rule set and bias "policy" over "policies"-whereas mid-dlPFC activity scales with the need to bind currently relevant cues to a chosen rule and suppress competitors 6. This posterior->anterior progression is supported by converging fMRI, lesion, and perturbation data, meta-analytic gradients, and formal accounts of hierarchical control.

Overlaid on this is a dorsal-ventral (and partially medial-lateral) specialization that clarifies the content of control. Dorsal LPFC is biased toward spatial/executive control and maintenance of spatial relations (e.g., oculomotor working memory, spatial selection), whereas ventrolateral PFC-especially left IFG/VLPFC-implements controlled retrieval and selection among competing semantic or feature representations (e.g., choosing the task-relevant meaning of an ambiguous word or feature dimension when competition is high) 7, 8, 9, 10. Medially, dACC/mpFC carries signals related to conflict, effort, and the expected value of deploying control, providing a motivational "meter" that tunes how strongly lateral PFC implements a chosen rule. On the ventral/medial side, vmPFC/OFC represents integrated subjective value 11 and OFC carries a cognitive map of latent task states-representations of "where you are" in an abstract state-space that guide flexible choice when the state isn’t directly observable. Together these gradients mean that a given task can recruit, in parallel, caudal sensorimotor codes to implement an S-R mapping, mid-lateral codes to maintain the current rule and suppress distractors, frontopolar codes to manage pending subgoals or explore alternatives, VLPFC codes to select among competing semantic/features, dACC signals to up- or down-regulate control intensity 12, and vmPFC/OFC state/value codes to bias choices under uncertainty.

These representational gradients align with macroscale connectivity. Along the brain’s principal connectivity gradient, anterior/medial PFC sits near the transmodal apex with the default‐mode network (DMN) 13, 1, while sensorimotor cortex anchors the opposite end; this arrangement predicts that anterior PFC will couple with memory/scene-construction machinery to support long-horizon goals, latent task states, and contextual priors. That’s what you see: during episodic retrieval and multi-step reasoning, anterior/rostrolateral PFC increases its functional coupling with hippocampus and DMN nodes, and overall network modularity drops as memory and control systems interlock-precisely the pattern you’d expect if PFC is binding a world-model to a control policy 14, 15, 16, 17.

At the other end of the hierarchy, caudal lateral PFC coactivates with dorsal attention (a "spotlight operator" network) and sensorimotor networks and is wired for concrete stimulus-response specifications and moment-to-moment selection 18. Bridging these poles, frontoparietal "flexible hubs" dynamically retune their connectivity-tightening links to DMN when internal models must be consulted, or to attention/sensorimotor systems when external constraints dominate-so the control system can route information through the right partners at the right time 18. Large meta-analytic gradient work in LPFC, together with flexible-hub studies, nails this picture: rostral bins lean DMN-ward, caudal bins lean DAN/sensorimotor-ward, and hub regions pivot between them as task demands shift 19.

Subcortically, similar axes organize control. The striatum exhibits a ventral-to-dorsal gradient: limbic and ventral striatum (nucleus accumbens) process reward prediction and goal valuation, whereas the posterior dorsolateral putamen (with contributions from caudate tail for over-learned visual habits) subserves learned stimulus-response habits 20, 21. Dopaminergic midbrain projections follow this scheme: the VTA predominantly innervates ventral/associative striatum while the SNc feeds dorsal striatum. Neocortical dopamine also shows gradients, with prefrontal cortex receiving dense modulatory input that tunes gating thresholds and plasticity 22, 23.

MD-PFC connectivity is topographic: anteromedial (’rostral’) MD links to frontal pole/medial PFC, lateral/parvocellular MD to dorsolateral PFC, and a caudodorsolateral MD sector to ACC/medial frontal cortex 24, 25; MD thus supports higher-order prefrontal state maintenance and routing. In parallel, VA/VL motor thalamus projects to premotor/motor cortex, and first-order sensory nuclei project to sensory cortices. The cerebellum shows a homologous gradient: anterior lobules couple with sensorimotor cortex, whereas Crus I/II and lobule VII couple with prefrontal association networks and support executive timing/prediction 26.
